section_summary: This section centers on the February 26, 1936 military uprising in Tokyo, its ideological and economic background, and its close relationship to the trials of Lieutenant Colonel Saburō Aizawa for murdering General Tetsuzan Nagata. It includes Embassy analyses, a detailed chronology of the coup, internal memoranda, and reports on the subsequent death sentence imposed on Aizawa. Later documents concern expansion of Japanese forces and barracks in North China, proposed controls on military and industrial information, and the Diet controversy over seditious-literature and mobilization-secrets legislation.

subfiles.title: Trial of Lieutenant-Colonel Saburo Aizawa and Its Political Significance
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports on Aizawa's first court-martial and connects its political revelations to the February 26 uprising.
subfiles.summary: Grew describes Aizawa's admitted murder of General Nagata, the conduct of the public trial, and the defense's presentation of the killing as an act inspired by the Shōwa Restoration movement. The testimony exposed hostility toward senior statesmen, financial magnates, bureaucrats, and the Army's moderate leadership while implicating numerous radical officers and civilian associates. Grew concludes that the emotionally charged proceedings probably helped precipitate the February 26 uprising and documents the influence of General Masaki on the younger officers.

subfiles.title: Document file note for Tokyo Telegram No. 38
subfiles.about: Indexes a telegram describing the February 26 coup and negotiations with the insurgents.
subfiles.summary: The sheet directs readers to file 894.00/566 for Tokyo Telegram No. 38. Its précis identifies the revolt as the work of companies of the First Division and notes that the Army High Command was negotiating to avoid further bloodshed and street fighting.

subfiles.title: Attempted Coup d'État in Tokyo, Telegram No. 38
subfiles.about: Provides a confidential early account of the forces, assassinations, occupied buildings, and negotiations in the February 26 coup.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy reports that roughly one thousand men from the First and Third Regiments of the First Division seized government buildings and attacked leading officials. It records confused reports about the victims, discussions over an acting premier, insurgent preferences for Kanji Katō or Hiranuma, and the movement of loyal troops into Tokyo. Grew emphasizes that the uprising was led by junior officers and was chauvinistic but had produced no anti-foreign demonstrations.

subfiles.title: Document file note for Despatch No. 1718
subfiles.about: Indexes a despatch analyzing the causes of the attempted Japanese military coup.
subfiles.summary: The file note identifies Despatch No. 1718 and directs readers to file 894.00/623. It characterizes the referenced document as an analysis of the causes leading to the February 26 coup.

subfiles.title: Analysis of the Causes of the February 26 Military Uprising
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Analyzes the long-term grievances, military ideology, and immediate triggers behind the February 26 uprising.
subfiles.summary: The despatch traces the revolt to tensions produced by industrialization, rural poverty, unequal wealth, hostility toward capitalists and senior statesmen, dissatisfaction with international treaties, and the Army's conception of the national polity. It argues that military spiritual training encouraged young officers to treat personal loyalty to the Emperor as superior to obedience to commanders, thereby legitimizing direct action in their own minds. Immediate triggers included the First Division's impending transfer to Manchuria, the Aizawa trial, and hostility to the Okada Cabinet. Grew anticipates efforts to restore discipline while warning that further unrest will remain likely unless economic grievances are addressed.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation with Dr. James A. B. Scherer
subfiles.about: Records Scherer's interpretation of General Masaki, Army factionalism, capitalism, and the causes of the uprising.
subfiles.summary: Scherer, describing himself as an intimate friend of Masaki, interprets the crisis through the May 15 incident, the alleged 1934 plot, Masaki's dismissal, and Nagata's assassination. He portrays the government as dominated by wealthy families and senior statesmen and presents Masaki as an opponent of plutocracy who favored agrarian and working-class rehabilitation. Scherer nevertheless states that Masaki had no advance knowledge of the uprising and believed in military discipline. The memorandum also records his belief that the First Division's impending departure for Manchuria drove the officers to act quickly.

subfiles.title: Document file note for Despatch No. 1721
subfiles.about: Indexes a sixteen-page despatch chronicling the February 26 uprising through March 6.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies Despatch No. 1721 and directs the reader to file 894.00/620. It states that the despatch forwards a chronological account of the uprising through noon on March 6.

subfiles.title: Chronicle of the February 26 Uprising Through March 6, 1936
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Presents a day-by-day narrative of the February 26 revolt, its suppression, and the subsequent political crisis.
subfiles.summary: The despatch reconstructs the seizure of official buildings, attacks on Saitō, Takahashi, Watanabe, Suzuki, and Okada's residence, the institution of martial law, censorship, and negotiations with the insurgents. It follows the Imperial command to disband, the surrender of enlisted men, the isolation and arrest of the remaining officers, and the restoration of normal communications and traffic. Later entries cover official investigations, Cabinet-formation difficulties, revelations that Okada survived, and ceremonies for the dead. A final page lists the proclamations, communiqués, newspaper extras, and other enclosures accompanying the original despatch.

subfiles.title: Document file note for Far Eastern Division memorandum on the February 26 coup
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Indexes a memorandum interpreting the coup as part of the military's effort to dominate Japanese state affairs.
subfiles.summary: The note refers readers to file 894.00/627 for the underlying memorandum. Its précis says the memorandum examines the Army's connection with the coup, possible effects on Japan's international relations, and the reaction then setting in.

subfiles.title: Document file note for Despatch No. 1693
subfiles.about: Indexes a report on the public trial of Aizawa for killing General Nagata.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies Despatch No. 1693 and refers readers to another State Department file. Its subject précis names Aizawa, Nagata, the August 1935 assassination, and the public court-martial.

subfiles.title: The Army: Public Trial of Lieutenant Colonel Saburo Aizawa
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Summarizes the opening phase and political implications of Aizawa's first public trial.
subfiles.summary: The extract outlines the indictment's claim that Aizawa came to view Nagata as an obstacle to national and Army reform, particularly after Masaki's dismissal. It records the defense warning that other direct-action officers would appear unless Aizawa's supposedly patriotic spirit was understood. The report notes that press interest centered on Aizawa's allegations that Nagata had allied with senior statesmen, bureaucrats, and wealthy interests.

subfiles.title: Document file note on proposed restrictions protecting Japanese commercial information
subfiles.about: Indexes a report on proposed Japanese restrictions on disclosure and aerial photography of factories and vital centers.
subfiles.summary: The note refers to a report concerning legislation intended to prevent disclosure of commercial information about Japanese factories. It specifically says that aerial photography of vital centers such as Tokyo, Osaka, and Nagoya would be prohibited.

subfiles.title: Document file note for Peiping Telegram No. 217
subfiles.about: Indexes a telegram concerning changes in the status of Japanese forces in Hebei and Beijing.
subfiles.summary: The note summarizes changes intended to demonstrate the Japanese military's fixed determination and enhance Lieutenant General Tada's status. It mentions both the North China Garrison and the Japanese Embassy Guard at Beijing.

subfiles.title: Changes in the Status of Japanese Forces in North China, Telegram No. 217
subfiles.about: Reports the elevation and expansion of Japanese military commands in Hebei and Beijing.
subfiles.summary: Johnson reports that the North China Garrison commander would henceforth receive a direct Imperial appointment, placing the position on a level with commanders in Kwantung, Korea, and Taiwan. Lieutenant General Tada was expected to receive the first appointment as the garrison doubled in strength. The Japanese Embassy Guard at Beijing was to become a brigade, adding an unusually large concentration of senior officers alongside Major General Matsumuro's military mission.

subfiles.title: Document file note for Peiping Telegram No. 240
subfiles.about: Indexes a telegram on construction of new Japanese barracks at Tianjin.
subfiles.summary: The sheet directs the reader to file 793.94/7898 for Telegram No. 240. Its subject line states that the telegram provides detailed information about new barracks for the Japanese garrison at Tianjin.

subfiles.title: Construction of New Japanese Barracks at Tientsin, Telegram No. 240
subfiles.about: Reports the scale and rapid progress of barracks construction for an expected Japanese troop increase at Tianjin.
subfiles.summary: Confidential commercial information indicated that Japanese contractors had obtained 750,000 feet of lumber for barracks expected to house five thousand troops arriving in June. A second contract for 300,000 feet was thought to cover an enlargement or an aerodrome. The Consul General reported that ten or more buildings and their access roads were already nearing completion.

subfiles.title: Document file note on naval construction and fortifications
subfiles.about: Indexes a telegram concerning Japanese concern about the cost of a fortification and naval-construction race.
subfiles.summary: The note refers to Tokyo Telegram No. 106. It says newspapers quoted the Navy Minister before the Diet Budget Committee as expressing apprehension about the cost of a possible race in fortifications and ship construction.

subfiles.title: Departmental note on Aizawa's death sentence
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes Tokyo Despatch No. 1821 concerning Aizawa's death sentence and appeal.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes that Aizawa was sentenced to death for murdering General Nagata and had appealed to a higher court-martial. It emphasizes the significance of the sentence in light of past leniency toward political assassins and the sympathetic atmosphere of Aizawa's first trial before the February 26 incident.

subfiles.title: Second Trial and Death Sentence of Lieutenant Colonel Aizawa
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports Aizawa's secret retrial, death sentence, and appeal to a higher court-martial.
subfiles.summary: Grew explains that the first trial was postponed by the February 26 uprising and that the lapse required a complete retrial. Uzawa withdrew as counsel, and five new hearings beginning April 22 were held in camera because publicity was said to threaten public order. Aizawa received a death sentence on May 7 and appealed on May 8. Grew interprets the result as possible evidence that the War Minister intended to reestablish discipline and punish direct-action methods.

subfiles.title: War Office Statement on the Aizawa Case
subfiles.about: Prints the War Office's explanation of Aizawa's motives, guilt, and lack of accomplices.
subfiles.summary: The statement calls Aizawa personally pure and loyal but simple, prejudiced, and susceptible to secret publications and irresponsible claims. It rejects his allegations that Nagata conspired with senior statesmen, bureaucrats, and financial leaders and says the evidence did not support the supposed intrigues. The Army presents the murder chiefly as a grave violation of discipline and asserts that Aizawa acted alone without instigators.

subfiles.title: Departmental digest of Tokyo Despatch No. 1876
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.to: Under Secretary of State William Phillips
subfiles.about: Summarizes the Diet struggle over the Seditious Literature and Mobilization Secrets bills.
subfiles.summary: The digest reports that the Seditious Literature Bill passed only after extensive revision while the Mobilization Secrets Bill failed. It characterizes both as reactionary measures backed by the Hirota Cabinet and opposed by the Diet, press, and public as threats to speech and individual liberty. The memorandum concludes that the controversy revealed a healthier and less docile public mood after February 26 than the government's proposals suggested.

subfiles.title: Seditious Literature Bill and Mobilization Secrets Bill
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Analyzes opposition to two Hirota Cabinet bills expanding controls over publications and military-industrial information.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy describes the bills as the outstanding controversy of the 69th Diet session: one sought to suppress anonymous or uncensored literature considered disruptive of Army discipline, the financial system, or public order, while the other would strengthen protection of military and industrial secrets. Opposition parties argued that existing law was sufficient and that repression would not cure the underlying social and military causes of unrest. Government ministers defended limited restrictions as necessary to restore public peace after February 26, but the Mobilization Secrets Bill was abandoned and the literature measure passed only after its penalties were reduced and its emergency character emphasized. The despatch interprets the struggle as a broader contest between liberal government and the combined pressures of bureaucracy and militarism.
